Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

vignette: The rain had come down in sheets over the Blue Ridge foothills, turning a dry creek bed into a violent, churning torrent before Kwame’s twenty-four-year-old brother could scramble to higher ground. Kwame had stood on the muddy bank, watching the brown water surge around his brother’s waist, then his chest, pulling him under with a terrifying finality that left only the smell of wet slate and decaying leaves hanging in the damp air. He had reached for him, his fingers grasping nothing but cold, rushing liquid, and the sudden, absolute silence that followed the splash became the anchor of his life. What he had come to believe was that the world could turn fatal in the span of a single breath, and that the water itself had become a quiet, waiting predator. In the months that followed, Kwame, a fifty-nine-year-old literature professor, found his daily routine unraveling. He could not walk past the campus lake without his pulse hammering against his ribs before his conscious mind could even register that it was merely a decorative pond. The damp, mineral scent of storm drains or a leaky radiator in his departmental office would send a jolt of cold dread straight through him. He tried to maintain his seminars, but the mounting stress of tenure reviews and grading piles acted as a quiet accelerant. His body would brace for impact, shoulders locking, breath catching, long before his thoughts could catch up. Negative emotions arrived unbidden—a thick wave of horror at a student’s casual remark about river rafting, followed by a sharp, familiar current of guilt that he had not pulled harder, or reached faster. The inability to relax settled into his posture; even in his quiet apartment, his muscles remained wound tight, as if expecting another surge to come at any moment. Over time, this pattern calcified into a relentless loop that dictated his existence, forming the structural backbone of his days. The moment the sight of rain gathering on his office window or the smell of damp wool from a colleague’s coat crossed his line of sight, his autonomic nervous system fired without warning, flooding him with tension and a profound inability to relax. His body’s premature alarm did not end there; it actively tuned his perception to hunt for more water and more stress, turning ordinary academic routines into potential hazards. When the dread spiked, his hypersensitivity sharpened, making him bristle at the sound of a sprinkler system or the clack of heavy boots on wet pavement, which in turn triggered another round of physical alarm and shame. The more his body reacted, the more he scanned his environment for the slightest hint of a rising tide or a stressful deadline, and the more his physiological dread would flare in response, until the boundaries between past and present dissolved completely. The consequences of this exhaustion were concrete and isolating. He began taking alternate routes through campus, afraid that proximity to standing water would spark another physical alarm, and he declined invitations to faculty retreats that involved lakes or even large decorative fountains. His single status, once a matter of personal preference, now felt like a necessary buffer; he could not bear the thought of subjecting a partner to the sudden withdrawals of his attention or the unexplained flinches that came with a passing glance at a glass of water. Now, sitting in the quiet of his therapist’s office, Kwame admits that he is seeking help because the fatigue has become heavier than the guilt, and he no longer recognizes the man who once taught with steady calm. He is afraid that the loop will tighten until he can no longer teach or leave his home, but what he most hopes for is simply to feel safe in his own skin again, to let his body stop sounding the alarm for a storm that ended years ago.
